strings.b-00-meta.title: Electricity: current, resistance, circuits and power
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.0: After this lesson you can explain what electric current is, state its unit, and use I = Q/t to find the charge flowing in a circuit.
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.1: After this lesson you can define potential difference and resistance, state Ohm's law, and calculate with V = IR and R = ρl/A.
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.2: After this lesson you can find the equivalent resistance of resistors joined in series or in parallel and solve circuit problems with them.
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.3: After this lesson you can calculate the heat produced by a current using H = I²Rt and the power and energy used by a device, including the cost in kilowatt hours.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.0.definition: The SI unit of electric charge; one coulomb is nearly the charge of 6 × 10^18 electrons.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.1.definition: The SI unit of electric current; one ampere is one coulomb of charge flowing per second.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.2.definition: The SI unit of potential difference; one volt is one joule of work per coulomb of charge moved.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.3.definition: The SI unit of resistance; a conductor has resistance 1 ohm when a potential difference of 1 volt drives a current of 1 ampere through it.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.4.definition: A property of the material of a conductor, with SI unit Ω m, that tells how strongly that material resists current for a given length and area.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.5.definition: The single resistance that can replace a combination of resistors while keeping the same current and potential difference for the whole circuit.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.6.definition: The rule H = I²Rt giving the heat produced in a resistor by a steady current.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.7.definition: The SI unit of power; one watt is consumed when a current of 1 ampere flows at a potential difference of 1 volt.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.8.definition: The commercial unit of electrical energy, equal to 3.6 × 10^6 J.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.9.definition: A short wire of suitable melting point placed in series with a device, which melts and breaks the circuit when the current becomes too large.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.0: You have seen a torch work. The cells inside push charge through the bulb, and the bulb glows only while the switch is on. Water flowing in a river is called a water current; in the same way, when electric charge flows through a conductor such as a metallic wire, we say there is an electric current in the conductor.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.1: A switch makes a conducting link between the cell and the bulb. If the circuit is broken anywhere, the current stops flowing and the bulb does not glow. A continuous and closed path of an electric current is called an electric circuit.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.2: Electric current is the amount of charge flowing through a particular area in unit time; in other words it is the rate of flow of electric charges. In metallic wires, electrons are the charges that flow. Electrons were not known when electricity was first observed, so current was taken to be the flow of positive charges, and by convention the direction of electric current is opposite to the direction of flow of electrons.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.3: If a net charge Q flows across any cross-section of a conductor in time t, then I = Q/t. The SI unit of charge is the coulomb (C), nearly the charge of 6 × 10^18 electrons, and an electron has a negative charge of 1.6 × 10^-19 C. The SI unit of current is the ampere (A), where 1 A = 1 C/1 s; small currents are written as 1 mA = 10^-3 A or 1 µA = 10^-6 A.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.4: An instrument called the ammeter measures electric current, and it is always connected in series in the circuit through which the current is to be measured. In the torch circuit the current flows from the positive terminal of the cell to the negative terminal through the bulb and the ammeter.
strings.b-02.caption: A simple circuit: a cell, a bulb, an ammeter and a plug key, all in one closed loop. Current leaves the positive terminal of the cell, goes through the bulb and the ammeter, and returns to the negative terminal.
strings.b-03.problem: A current of 0.5 A is drawn by a filament of an electric bulb for 10 minutes. Find the amount of electric charge that flows through the circuit.
strings.b-03.steps.0.title: Write down what is given
strings.b-03.steps.0.detail: Current I = 0.5 A. Time t = 10 minutes.
strings.b-03.steps.1.title: Put the time in seconds
strings.b-03.steps.1.detail: t = 10 min = 10 × 60 s = 600 s, because the ampere is coulombs per second.
strings.b-03.steps.2.title: Use the definition of current
strings.b-03.steps.2.detail: I = Q/t, so Q = I × t.
strings.b-03.steps.3.title: Substitute
strings.b-03.answer: The amount of charge that flows through the circuit is 300 C.
strings.b-04.question: What does an electric circuit mean?
strings.b-04.options.0: A continuous and closed path of an electric current
strings.b-04.options.1: A path that is broken at the switch
strings.b-04.options.2: Any piece of metal that carries charge
strings.b-04.options.3: The flow of electrons from the positive terminal to the negative terminal
strings.b-04.explanation: A switch makes a conducting link between the cell and the bulb, so the path must be closed; if the circuit is broken anywhere the current stops and the bulb does not glow. Note also that electrons are negative, so the conventional current is taken opposite to the direction of electron flow, not along it.
strings.b-05.question: Calculate the number of electrons constituting one coulomb of charge.
strings.b-05.explanation: One electron carries a charge of 1.6 × 10^-19 C. So the number of electrons in 1 C is 1 / (1.6 × 10^-19), which is about 6.25 × 10^18, that is nearly 6 × 10^18 electrons. This is exactly why one coulomb is said to be the charge contained in nearly 6 × 10^18 electrons.
strings.b-06.paragraphs.0: Charges do not flow in a copper wire by themselves, just as water in a perfectly horizontal tube does not flow. If one end of the tube is joined to a tank kept at a higher level, so that there is a pressure difference between the two ends, water flows out of the other end.
strings.b-06.paragraphs.1: For charges in a metallic wire, gravity has no role to play. The electrons move only if there is a difference of electric pressure, called the potential difference, along the conductor. A battery, made of one or more cells, produces this difference.
strings.b-06.paragraphs.2: The chemical action within a cell generates the potential difference across its terminals even when no current is drawn from it. When the cell is connected to a conducting circuit element, the potential difference sets the charges in motion and produces an electric current, and to keep the current flowing the cell has to expend its stored chemical energy.
strings.b-06.paragraphs.3: The potential difference between two points in a circuit carrying some current is the work done to move a unit charge from one point to the other, so V = W/Q. Its SI unit is the volt (V): one volt is the potential difference between two points when 1 joule of work is done to move a charge of 1 coulomb, that is 1 V = 1 J C^-1.
strings.b-06.paragraphs.4: The voltmeter measures potential difference, and it is always connected in parallel across the points between which the potential difference is to be measured.
strings.b-07.problem: How much work is done in moving a charge of 2 C across two points having a potential difference 12 V?
strings.b-07.steps.0.title: Write down what is given
strings.b-07.steps.0.detail: Charge Q = 2 C, potential difference V = 12 V.
strings.b-07.steps.1.title: Use the definition of potential difference
strings.b-07.steps.1.detail: V = W/Q, so the work done is W = V × Q.
strings.b-07.steps.2.title: Substitute
strings.b-08.question: How much energy is given to each coulomb of charge passing through a 6 V battery?
strings.b-08.explanation: One volt means one joule of work per coulomb, so a 6 V battery gives 6 J of energy to every coulomb that passes through it. The battery is the device that maintains this potential difference across the conductor.
strings.b-09.paragraphs.0: A circuit contains a cell or a battery, a plug key, the electrical components and connecting wires. Instead of drawing the real objects, we draw a schematic diagram in which each component is replaced by a conventional symbol.
strings.b-09.paragraphs.1: The symbols you will meet are: an electric cell; a battery, which is a combination of cells; a plug key or switch, shown open or closed; a wire joint; wires crossing without joining; an electric bulb; a resistor of resistance R; a variable resistance or rheostat; an ammeter; and a voltmeter.
strings.b-09.paragraphs.2: Two of these symbols carry a rule with them. The ammeter goes in series with the part whose current you are measuring, and the voltmeter goes in parallel with the part whose potential difference you are measuring.
strings.b-10.question: How is a voltmeter connected in the circuit to measure the potential difference between two points?
strings.b-10.options.0: In parallel across the two points
strings.b-10.explanation: A voltmeter is always connected in parallel across the points between which the potential difference is to be measured. The ammeter is the one that goes in series, because it must carry the current it is measuring.
strings.b-11.paragraphs.0: Set up a circuit with a nichrome wire XY of length about 0.5 m, an ammeter, a voltmeter and four cells of 1.5 V each. Start with one cell and note the ammeter reading I and the voltmeter reading V across XY; then repeat with two, three and four cells. For each pair, work out V/I, and plot V against I.
strings.b-11.paragraphs.1: In the activity you find approximately the same value of V/I in every case, and the V-I graph is a straight line passing through the origin. So V/I is a constant ratio for that wire.
strings.b-11.paragraphs.2: In 1827 the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm found the relationship between the current in a metallic wire and the potential difference across its ends. The potential difference V across the ends of a given metallic wire is directly proportional to the current I through it, provided its temperature remains the same. This is Ohm's law: V is proportional to I, so V/I = constant = R, and V = IR.
strings.b-11.paragraphs.3: R is a constant for the given metallic wire at a given temperature and is called its resistance, the property of a conductor to resist the flow of charges through it. Its SI unit is the ohm (Ω). If the potential difference across a conductor is 1 V and the current through it is 1 A, its resistance is 1 Ω, that is 1 ohm = 1 volt/1 ampere.
strings.b-11.paragraphs.4: Because V = IR can be written I = V/R, the current through a resistor is inversely proportional to its resistance: if the resistance is doubled the current gets halved. In many practical cases we need to increase or decrease the current, and a component used to regulate current without changing the voltage source is called a variable resistance; a device called a rheostat is often used in a circuit to change the resistance.
strings.b-12.title: V-I graph of a nichrome wire
strings.b-12.description: A nichrome wire is connected to a number of 1.5 V cells, with an ammeter and a voltmeter. Add cells and change the wire resistance, and watch where each (current, potential difference) point falls on the graph.
strings.b-12.controls.cells.label: Cells in the circuit (1.5 V each)
strings.b-12.controls.resistance.label: Resistance of the wire (ohm)
strings.b-13.problem: (a) How much current will an electric bulb draw from a 220 V source, if the resistance of the bulb filament is 1200 Ω? (b) How much current will an electric heater coil draw from a 220 V source, if the resistance of the heater coil is 100 Ω?
strings.b-13.steps.0.title: Write down what is given for the bulb
strings.b-13.steps.1.title: Use Ohm's law in the form I = V/R
strings.b-13.steps.2.title: Write down what is given for the heater
strings.b-13.steps.3.title: Use I = V/R again
strings.b-13.answer: The bulb draws about 0.18 A and the heater coil draws 2.2 A from the same 220 V source. Note the difference of current drawn by a bulb and a heater from the same source: the smaller the resistance, the larger the current.
strings.b-14.problem: The potential difference between the terminals of an electric heater is 60 V when it draws a current of 4 A from the source. What current will the heater draw if the potential difference is increased to 120 V?
strings.b-14.steps.0.title: Find the resistance first
strings.b-14.steps.0.detail: The resistance of the heater stays the same. From Ohm's law, R = V/I = 60 V / 4 A = 15 Ω.
strings.b-14.steps.1.title: Now change the potential difference
strings.b-14.steps.1.detail: With V = 120 V and R = 15 Ω, the current is I = V/R.
strings.b-14.steps.2.title: Substitute
strings.b-14.answer: The current through the heater becomes 8 A when the potential difference is doubled.
strings.b-15.question: When a 12 V battery is connected across an unknown resistor, there is a current of 2.5 mA in the circuit. Find the value of the resistance of the resistor, in ohms.
strings.b-15.explanation: First change the current to amperes: 2.5 mA = 2.5 × 10^-3 A. Then R = V/I = 12 V / (2.5 × 10^-3 A) = 4800 Ω.
strings.b-16.paragraphs.0: Take a circuit with a cell, an ammeter, a nichrome wire of length l and a plug key, and note the current. Now replace the wire with another nichrome wire of the same thickness but twice the length, and note the current again: the ammeter reading decreases to one-half.
strings.b-16.paragraphs.1: Repeat with a thicker nichrome wire of the same length, so that its cross-sectional area is larger: the ammeter reading increases. Now use a copper wire of the same length and the same area of cross-section as the first nichrome wire, and the reading changes again.
strings.b-16.paragraphs.2: These observations show that the resistance of a conductor depends on its length, on its area of cross-section, and on the nature of its material. Precise measurements show that the resistance of a uniform metallic conductor is directly proportional to its length l and inversely proportional to its area of cross-section A, so R = ρl/A.
strings.b-16.paragraphs.3: The constant ρ (rho) is called the electrical resistivity of the material of the conductor. Its SI unit is Ω m, and it is a characteristic property of the material. Metals and alloys have very low resistivity, in the range 10^-8 Ω m to 10^-6 Ω m, and are good conductors of electricity; insulators like rubber and glass have resistivity of the order of 10^12 to 10^17 Ω m. Both the resistance and the resistivity of a material vary with temperature.
strings.b-16.paragraphs.4: The resistivity of an alloy is generally higher than that of its constituent metals, and alloys do not oxidise (burn) readily at high temperatures; for this reason they are commonly used in electrical heating devices like electric irons and toasters. Tungsten is used almost exclusively for filaments of electric bulbs, while copper and aluminium are generally used for electrical transmission lines.
strings.b-17.problem: Resistance of a metal wire of length 1 m is 26 Ω at 20 degrees C. If the diameter of the wire is 0.3 mm, what will be the resistivity of the metal at that temperature? Using the table of resistivities, predict the material of the wire.
strings.b-17.steps.0.title: Write down what is given
strings.b-17.steps.0.detail: R = 26 Ω, length l = 1 m, diameter d = 0.3 mm = 3 × 10^-4 m.
strings.b-17.steps.1.title: Find the area of cross-section
strings.b-17.steps.1.detail: The wire is round, so A = πd²/4.
strings.b-17.steps.2.title: Rearrange R = ρl/A
strings.b-17.steps.2.detail: The resistivity is ρ = RA/l = Rπd²/(4l).
strings.b-17.steps.3.title: Substitute
strings.b-17.steps.3.detail: Putting in the values gives ρ = 1.84 × 10^-6 Ω m.
strings.b-17.steps.4.title: Name the material
strings.b-17.steps.4.detail: Looking at the table of resistivities at 20 degrees C, the value 1.84 × 10^-6 Ω m is the resistivity of manganese.
strings.b-17.answer: The resistivity of the metal at 20 degrees C is 1.84 × 10^-6 Ω m, which is the resistivity of manganese.
strings.b-18.problem: A wire of given material having length l and area of cross-section A has a resistance of 4 Ω. What would be the resistance of another wire of the same material having length l/2 and area of cross-section 2A?
strings.b-18.steps.0.title: Write the first wire
strings.b-18.steps.0.detail: For the first wire, R1 = ρl/A = 4 Ω.
strings.b-18.steps.1.title: Write the second wire
strings.b-18.steps.1.detail: For the second wire, R2 = ρ(l/2)/(2A) = (1/4) ρl/A.
strings.b-18.steps.2.title: Compare the two
strings.b-18.steps.3.title: Substitute
strings.b-18.answer: The resistance of the new wire is 1 Ω.
strings.b-19.question: Will current flow more easily through a thick wire or a thin wire of the same material, when connected to the same source? Why?
strings.b-19.options.0: A thick wire, because a larger area of cross-section gives a smaller resistance
strings.b-19.options.1: A thin wire, because a smaller area of cross-section gives a smaller resistance
strings.b-19.options.2: Both equally, because the material is the same
strings.b-19.options.3: A thick wire, because the material of a thick wire has lower resistivity
strings.b-19.explanation: Resistance is inversely proportional to the area of cross-section, R = ρl/A. A thicker wire of the same material and length has the larger area, so its resistance is smaller and the current is larger. Resistivity depends on the material only, not on the thickness.
strings.b-20.paragraphs.0: When three resistors R1, R2 and R3 are joined end to end, they are said to be connected in series. If you move the ammeter to any position in such a circuit, its reading does not change: in a series combination the current is the same in every part of the circuit, so the same current passes through each resistor.
strings.b-20.paragraphs.1: Measure the potential difference across the whole combination and call it V, then measure the potential differences V1, V2 and V3 across the three resistors separately. You find that V = V1 + V2 + V3: the total potential difference across a series combination is the sum of the potential differences across the individual resistors.
strings.b-20.paragraphs.2: Now replace the three resistors by one equivalent resistor of resistance R that carries the same current I with the same potential difference V across it, so that V = IR. Applying Ohm's law to the three resistors separately gives V1 = IR1, V2 = IR2 and V3 = IR3.
strings.b-20.paragraphs.3: Putting these into V = V1 + V2 + V3 gives IR = IR1 + IR2 + IR3, and dividing by I gives Rs = R1 + R2 + R3. So when several resistors are joined in series, the resistance of the combination equals the sum of their individual resistances, and it is greater than any individual resistance.
strings.b-21.caption: Resistors in series: the three resistors are joined end to end between X and Y, so the same current I passes through each of them. The potential differences add up: V = V1 + V2 + V3.
strings.b-22.title: Why Rs = R1 + R2 + R3
strings.b-22.steps.0.title: Start from the observed sum
strings.b-22.steps.0.detail: The experiment shows the total potential difference is V = V1 + V2 + V3 across the series combination.
strings.b-22.steps.1.title: Replace the combination by one resistor
strings.b-22.steps.1.detail: Let one equivalent resistor R carry the same current I with the same total potential difference V, so Ohm's law for the whole circuit gives V = IR.
strings.b-22.steps.2.title: Apply Ohm's law to each resistor
strings.b-22.steps.2.detail: The current through each resistor is the same I, so V1 = IR1, V2 = IR2 and V3 = IR3.
strings.b-22.steps.3.title: Substitute and cancel I
strings.b-22.steps.3.detail: IR = IR1 + IR2 + IR3, and dividing both sides by I gives Rs = R1 + R2 + R3.
strings.b-22.steps.4.title: Read the result
strings.b-22.steps.4.detail: The equivalent resistance is the plain sum, so it is larger than any single resistance in the combination.
strings.b-23.problem: An electric lamp, whose resistance is 20 Ω, and a conductor of 4 Ω resistance are connected to a 6 V battery. Calculate (a) the total resistance of the circuit, (b) the current through the circuit, and (c) the potential difference across the electric lamp and conductor.
strings.b-23.steps.0.title: Add the series resistances
strings.b-23.steps.0.detail: The lamp R1 = 20 Ω and the conductor R2 = 4 Ω are in series, so Rs = 20 Ω + 4 Ω = 24 Ω.
strings.b-23.steps.1.title: Find the current
strings.b-23.steps.1.detail: The battery gives V = 6 V, so I = V/Rs = 6 V / 24 Ω = 0.25 A. This same current flows through both.
strings.b-23.steps.2.title: Potential difference across the lamp
strings.b-23.steps.3.title: Potential difference across the conductor
strings.b-23.steps.3.detail: V2 = R2 × I = 4 Ω × 0.25 A = 1 V. Check: 5 V + 1 V = 6 V, the battery voltage.
strings.b-23.steps.4.title: Check the equivalent resistance
strings.b-23.steps.4.detail: A single resistor replacing the two must give 0.25 A at 6 V, so R = V/I = 6 V / 0.25 A = 24 Ω, the same as the total series resistance.
strings.b-23.answer: Total resistance 24 Ω, current 0.25 A, potential difference 5 V across the lamp and 1 V across the conductor.
strings.b-24.question: A battery of three cells of 2 V each is connected in series with a 5 Ω resistor, an 8 Ω resistor, a 12 Ω resistor and a plug key. What current flows through the resistors? Give the answer in amperes.
strings.b-24.explanation: Three cells of 2 V each give 6 V. The series resistance is 5 + 8 + 12 = 25 Ω. So I = V/Rs = 6 V / 25 Ω = 0.24 A, and this same current flows through every resistor. A voltmeter connected across the 12 Ω resistor would read 12 Ω × 0.24 A = 2.88 V.
strings.b-25.paragraphs.0: When three resistors are connected together between the same two points X and Y, they are said to be connected in parallel. Now the potential difference across each resistor is the same, but the current divides.
strings.b-25.paragraphs.1: Measure the total current I entering the combination, and then the separate currents I1, I2 and I3 through the three branches. You find I = I1 + I2 + I3: the total current is the sum of the separate currents through each branch of the combination.
strings.b-25.paragraphs.2: Let Rp be the equivalent resistance of the parallel combination. Applying Ohm's law to the whole combination gives I = V/Rp, and applying it to each resistor gives I1 = V/R1, I2 = V/R2 and I3 = V/R3.
strings.b-25.paragraphs.3: Substituting these into I = I1 + I2 + I3 gives V/Rp = V/R1 + V/R2 + V/R3, and dividing by V gives 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. The reciprocal of the equivalent resistance of a group of resistors joined in parallel equals the sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances, so the total resistance in a parallel circuit is decreased.
strings.b-25.paragraphs.4: The two arrangements behave very differently. In a series circuit the current is constant throughout, so it is impracticable to connect an electric bulb and an electric heater in series, because they need currents of widely different values to operate properly. Another disadvantage of a series circuit is that when one component fails the circuit is broken and none of the components works, as you see when a single dead bulb in a string of fairy lights puts out the whole string. A parallel circuit, on the other hand, divides the current through the gadgets, which helps when each gadget has a different resistance and needs a different current.
strings.b-26.caption: Resistors in parallel: the three resistors are connected between the same two points X and Y, so each one has the same potential difference V across it, while the total current divides into I1, I2 and I3.
strings.b-27.title: Why 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3
strings.b-27.steps.0.title: Start from the observed sum
strings.b-27.steps.0.detail: The experiment shows the total current is I = I1 + I2 + I3 into the parallel combination.
strings.b-27.steps.1.title: Replace the combination by one resistor
strings.b-27.steps.1.detail: Let one equivalent resistor Rp carry the same total current I at the same potential difference V, so I = V/Rp.
strings.b-27.steps.2.title: Apply Ohm's law to each branch
strings.b-27.steps.2.detail: Every branch has the same potential difference V, so I1 = V/R1, I2 = V/R2 and I3 = V/R3.
strings.b-27.steps.3.title: Substitute and cancel V
strings.b-27.steps.3.detail: V/Rp = V/R1 + V/R2 + V/R3, and dividing both sides by V gives 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3.
strings.b-27.steps.4.title: Read the result
strings.b-27.steps.4.detail: We add the reciprocals, so the equivalent resistance comes out smaller than the smallest individual resistance.
strings.b-28.problem: Three resistors R1, R2 and R3 have the values 5 Ω, 10 Ω and 30 Ω respectively, and are connected in parallel to a battery of 12 V. Calculate (a) the current through each resistor, (b) the total current in the circuit, and (c) the total circuit resistance.
strings.b-28.steps.0.title: Note the potential difference
strings.b-28.steps.0.detail: The battery gives V = 12 V, and this is also the potential difference across each individual resistor because they are in parallel.
strings.b-28.steps.1.title: Current through R1
strings.b-28.steps.2.title: Current through R2
strings.b-28.steps.3.title: Current through R3
strings.b-28.steps.4.title: Total current
strings.b-28.steps.5.title: Total resistance
strings.b-28.answer: The branch currents are 2.4 A, 1.2 A and 0.4 A; the total current is 4 A; the total resistance of the parallel combination is 3 Ω.
strings.b-29.problem: In a circuit with a 12 V battery, R1 = 10 Ω and R2 = 40 Ω are in parallel with each other, and R3 = 30 Ω, R4 = 20 Ω and R5 = 60 Ω are in parallel with each other; the two parallel groups are joined in series. Calculate (a) the total resistance in the circuit and (b) the total current flowing in the circuit.
strings.b-29.steps.0.title: Replace the first parallel pair
strings.b-29.steps.1.title: Replace the second parallel group
strings.b-29.steps.2.title: Add the two groups in series
strings.b-29.steps.2.detail: The total resistance is R = R' + R'' = 8 Ω + 10 Ω = 18 Ω.
strings.b-29.steps.3.title: Find the total current
strings.b-29.steps.3.detail: By Ohm's law, I = V/R = 12 V / 18 Ω = 0.67 A.
strings.b-29.answer: The total resistance is 18 Ω and the total current is about 0.67 A.
strings.b-30.question: What are the advantages of connecting electrical devices in parallel with the battery instead of connecting them in series?
strings.b-30.options.0: Each device works with the full source voltage and independently, and the total resistance of the circuit decreases
strings.b-30.options.1: The same current flows through every device
strings.b-30.options.2: When one device fails, all the other devices stop working
strings.b-30.options.3: The total resistance of the circuit increases as more devices are added
strings.b-30.explanation: In a parallel circuit every gadget gets the same potential difference and its own current, which suits gadgets of different resistances, and the total resistance is decreased. In a series circuit a single failure breaks the circuit and nothing works, which is why series wiring is not used for domestic circuits.
strings.b-31.paragraphs.0: A cell or battery is a source of electrical energy, and to maintain a current the source keeps expending energy. Part of that energy may be used in useful work, like rotating the blades of an electric fan, and the rest may be expended as heat, which is why a fan becomes warm when used continuously for a long time.
strings.b-31.paragraphs.1: If the electric circuit is purely resistive, that is, a configuration of resistors only connected to a battery, the source energy continually gets dissipated entirely in the form of heat. This is known as the heating effect of electric current, and it is used in devices such as electric heaters and electric irons.
strings.b-31.paragraphs.2: Consider a current I flowing through a resistor of resistance R with a potential difference V across it, and let a charge Q flow in time t. The work done in moving the charge Q through the potential difference V is VQ, so the source must supply energy VQ in time t, and the power input to the circuit is P = VQ/t = VI. The energy supplied by the source in time t is therefore VIt, and this energy is dissipated in the resistor as heat, so H = VIt.
strings.b-31.paragraphs.3: Applying Ohm's law V = IR to this gives H = I²Rt. strings.b-32.steps.0.title: Energy supplied by the source

strings.b-32.steps.1.title: Write the power input
strings.b-32.steps.1.detail: Since I = Q/t, the power input is P = VQ/t = VI, so the energy supplied in time t is VIt.
strings.b-32.steps.2.title: This energy becomes heat
strings.b-32.steps.2.detail: In a purely resistive circuit the whole of it is dissipated in the resistor as heat, so H = VIt.
strings.b-32.steps.3.title: Use Ohm's law to remove V
strings.b-32.steps.3.detail: Put V = IR into H = VIt, giving H = (IR)It = I²Rt.
strings.b-32.steps.4.title: Read the three proportionalities

strings.b-33.problem: An electric iron consumes energy at a rate of 840 W when heating is at the maximum rate and 360 W when the heating is at the minimum. The voltage is 220 V. What are the current and the resistance in each case?
strings.b-33.steps.0.title: Start from the power relation
strings.b-33.steps.0.detail: The power input is P = VI, so the current is I = P/V, and the resistance follows from R = V/I.
strings.b-33.steps.1.title: Maximum heating rate: current
strings.b-33.steps.2.title: Maximum heating rate: resistance
strings.b-33.steps.3.title: Minimum heating rate: current
strings.b-33.steps.4.title: Minimum heating rate: resistance
strings.b-33.answer: At the maximum rate the current is 3.82 A and the resistance is 57.60 Ω; at the minimum rate the current is 1.64 A and the resistance is 134.15 Ω.
strings.b-34.problem: 100 J of heat is produced each second in a 4 Ω resistance. Find the potential difference across the resistor.
strings.b-34.steps.0.title: Write down what is given
strings.b-34.steps.0.detail: Heat H = 100 J, resistance R = 4 Ω, time t = 1 s. We want V.
strings.b-34.steps.1.title: Use Joule's law to get the current
strings.b-34.steps.1.detail: H = I²Rt, so I = square root of (H / (Rt)) = square root of (100 J / (4 Ω × 1 s)) = 5 A.
strings.b-34.steps.2.title: Find the potential difference

strings.b-35.question: An electric iron of resistance 20 Ω takes a current of 5 A. Calculate the heat developed in 30 s. Give the answer in joules.

strings.b-39.steps.0.title: Write down what is given
strings.b-39.steps.1.title: Use the power relation
strings.b-39.steps.2.title: Substitute
strings.b-39.answer: The power of the bulb is 110 W.
strings.b-40.problem: An electric refrigerator rated 400 W operates 8 hour/day. What is the cost of the energy to operate it for 30 days at Rs 3.00 per kW h?
strings.b-40.steps.0.title: Find the total energy in watt hours
strings.b-40.steps.1.title: Convert to kilowatt hours
strings.b-40.steps.1.detail: 96000 W h = 96 kW h, since 1 kW h = 1000 W h.
strings.b-40.steps.2.title: Multiply by the rate

strings.b-41.question: Which of the following terms does not represent electrical power in a circuit?
strings.b-41.explanation: Electric power is P = VI, which becomes P = I²R when V = IR is put in, and P = V²/R when I = V/R is put in. The combination IR² has the wrong powers of I and R, so it is not a power.
strings.b-42.question: A piece of wire of resistance R is cut into five equal parts. These parts are then connected in parallel. If the equivalent resistance of this combination is R', then what is the ratio R/R'?
strings.b-42.explanation: Each of the five equal parts has resistance R/5. Five such resistors in parallel have 1/R' = 5/(R/5) = 25/R, so R' = R/25. Therefore R/R' = 25.
strings.b-43.question: An electric bulb is rated 220 V and 100 W. When it is operated on 110 V, what power will it consume?
strings.b-43.explanation: The resistance of the bulb is fixed: R = V²/P = (220 V)² / 100 W = 484 Ω. At 110 V the power is P = V²/R = (110 V)² / 484 Ω = 25 W. Halving the voltage quarters the power, because power goes as V² for a fixed resistance.
strings.b-44.question: Two conducting wires of the same material and of equal lengths and equal diameters are first connected in series and then in parallel in a circuit across the same potential difference. What is the ratio of the heat produced in the series combination to that in the parallel combination?
strings.b-44.explanation: Each wire has resistance R. In series the resistance is 2R; in parallel it is R/2. For the same potential difference V and the same time t, the heat is V²t/R, so it is inversely proportional to the resistance. The ratio of heats is (1/2R) : (1/(R/2)) = 1 : 4.
strings.b-45.question: How many 176 Ω resistors (in parallel) are required to carry 5 A on a 220 V line?
strings.b-45.explanation: The combination must have resistance R = V/I = 220 V / 5 A = 44 Ω. If n resistors of 176 Ω are joined in parallel, R = 176/n, so n = 176/44 = 4.

sections.title: Electric current and electric circuit
paragraphs: You have seen a torch work. The cells inside push charge through the bulb, and the bulb glows only while the switch is on. Water flowing in a river is called a water current; in the same way, when electric charge flows through a conductor such as a metallic wire, we say there is an electric current in the conductor.

A switch makes a conducting link between the cell and the bulb. If the circuit is broken anywhere, the current stops flowing and the bulb does not glow. A continuous and closed path of an electric current is called an electric circuit.

Electric current is the amount of charge flowing through a particular area in unit time; in other words it is the rate of flow of electric charges. In metallic wires, electrons are the charges that flow. Electrons were not known when electricity was first observed, so current was taken to be the flow of positive charges, and by convention the direction of electric current is opposite to the direction of flow of electrons.

If a net charge Q flows across any cross-section of a conductor in time t, then I = Q/t. The SI unit of charge is the coulomb (C), nearly the charge of 6 × 10^18 electrons, and an electron has a negative charge of 1.6 × 10^-19 C. The SI unit of current is the ampere (A), where 1 A = 1 C/1 s; small currents are written as 1 mA = 10^-3 A or 1 µA = 10^-6 A.

An instrument called the ammeter measures electric current, and it is always connected in series in the circuit through which the current is to be measured. In the torch circuit the current flows from the positive terminal of the cell to the negative terminal through the bulb and the ammeter.

sections.title: Electric potential and potential difference
paragraphs: Charges do not flow in a copper wire by themselves, just as water in a perfectly horizontal tube does not flow. If one end of the tube is joined to a tank kept at a higher level, so that there is a pressure difference between the two ends, water flows out of the other end.

For charges in a metallic wire, gravity has no role to play. The electrons move only if there is a difference of electric pressure, called the potential difference, along the conductor. A battery, made of one or more cells, produces this difference.

The chemical action within a cell generates the potential difference across its terminals even when no current is drawn from it. When the cell is connected to a conducting circuit element, the potential difference sets the charges in motion and produces an electric current, and to keep the current flowing the cell has to expend its stored chemical energy.

The potential difference between two points in a circuit carrying some current is the work done to move a unit charge from one point to the other, so V = W/Q. Its SI unit is the volt (V): one volt is the potential difference between two points when 1 joule of work is done to move a charge of 1 coulomb, that is 1 V = 1 J C^-1.
The voltmeter measures potential difference, and it is always connected in parallel across the points between which the potential difference is to be measured.

sections.title: Circuit diagrams and the symbols we use
paragraphs: A circuit contains a cell or a battery, a plug key, the electrical components and connecting wires. Instead of drawing the real objects, we draw a schematic diagram in which each component is replaced by a conventional symbol.

The symbols you will meet are: an electric cell; a battery, which is a combination of cells; a plug key or switch, shown open or closed; a wire joint; wires crossing without joining; an electric bulb; a resistor of resistance R; a variable resistance or rheostat; an ammeter; and a voltmeter.

Two of these symbols carry a rule with them. The ammeter goes in series with the part whose current you are measuring, and the voltmeter goes in parallel with the part whose potential difference you are measuring.

sections.title: Ohm's law and resistance
paragraphs: Set up a circuit with a nichrome wire XY of length about 0.5 m, an ammeter, a voltmeter and four cells of 1.5 V each. Start with one cell and note the ammeter reading I and the voltmeter reading V across XY; then repeat with two, three and four cells. For each pair, work out V/I, and plot V against I.
In the activity you find approximately the same value of V/I in every case, and the V-I graph is a straight line passing through the origin. So V/I is a constant ratio for that wire.

In 1827 the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm found the relationship between the current in a metallic wire and the potential difference across its ends. The potential difference V across the ends of a given metallic wire is directly proportional to the current I through it, provided its temperature remains the same. This is Ohm's law: V ∝ I, so V/I = constant = R, and V = IR.

R is a constant for the given metallic wire at a given temperature and is called its resistance, the property of a conductor to resist the flow of charges through it. Its SI unit is the ohm (Ω). If the potential difference across a conductor is 1 V and the current through it is 1 A, its resistance is 1 Ω, that is 1 ohm = 1 volt/1 ampere.

Because V = IR can be written I = V/R, the current through a resistor is inversely proportional to its resistance: if the resistance is doubled the current gets halved. In many practical cases we need to increase or decrease the current, and a component used to regulate current without changing the voltage source is called a variable resistance; a device called a rheostat is often used in a circuit to change the resistance.

sections.title: What decides the resistance of a conductor
paragraphs: Take a circuit with a cell, an ammeter, a nichrome wire of length l and a plug key. Note the current. Now replace the wire with another nichrome wire of the same thickness but twice the length, and note the current again: the ammeter reading decreases to one-half.

Repeat with a thicker nichrome wire of the same length, so that its cross-sectional area is larger: the ammeter reading increases. Now use a copper wire of the same length and the same area of cross-section as the first nichrome wire, and the reading changes again.

These observations show that the resistance of a conductor depends on its length, on its area of cross-section, and on the nature of its material. Precise measurements show that the resistance of a uniform metallic conductor is directly proportional to its length l and inversely proportional to its area of cross-section A, so R = ρl/A.

The constant ρ (rho) is called the electrical resistivity of the material of the conductor. Its SI unit is Ω m, and it is a characteristic property of the material. Metals and alloys have very low resistivity, in the range 10^-8 Ω m to 10^-6 Ω m, and are good conductors of electricity; insulators like rubber and glass have resistivity of the order of 10^12 to 10^17 Ω m. Both the resistance and the resistivity of a material vary with temperature.

The resistivity of an alloy is generally higher than that of its constituent metals, and alloys do not oxidise (burn) readily at high temperatures; for this reason they are commonly used in electrical heating devices like electric irons and toasters. Tungsten is used almost exclusively for filaments of electric bulbs, while copper and aluminium are generally used for electrical transmission lines. Nichrome, a common wire in these experiments, is an alloy of nickel, chromium, manganese and iron.

sections.title: Resistors joined in series
paragraphs: When three resistors R1, R2 and R3 are joined end to end, they are said to be connected in series. If you move the ammeter to any position in such a circuit, its reading does not change: in a series combination the current is the same in every part of the circuit, so the same current passes through each resistor.

Measure the potential difference across the whole combination and call it V, then measure the potential differences V1, V2 and V3 across the three resistors separately. You find that V = V1 + V2 + V3: the total potential difference across a series combination is the sum of the potential differences across the individual resistors.

Now replace the three resistors by one equivalent resistor of resistance R that carries the same current I with the same potential difference V across it, so that V = IR. Applying Ohm's law to the three resistors separately gives V1 = IR1, V2 = IR2 and V3 = IR3.

Putting these into V = V1 + V2 + V3 gives IR = IR1 + IR2 + IR3, and dividing by I gives Rs = R1 + R2 + R3. So when several resistors are joined in series, the resistance of the combination equals the sum of their individual resistances, and it is greater than any individual resistance.

sections.title: Resistors joined in parallel
paragraphs: When three resistors are connected together between the same two points X and Y, they are said to be connected in parallel. Now the potential difference across each resistor is the same, but the current divides.

Measure the total current I entering the combination, and then the separate currents I1, I2 and I3 through the three branches. You find I = I1 + I2 + I3: the total current is the sum of the separate currents through each branch of the combination.
Let Rp be the equivalent resistance of the parallel combination. Applying Ohm's law to the whole combination gives I = V/Rp, and applying it to each resistor gives I1 = V/R1, I2 = V/R2 and I3 = V/R3.

Substituting these into I = I1 + I2 + I3 gives V/Rp = V/R1 + V/R2 + V/R3, and dividing by V gives 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. The reciprocal of the equivalent resistance of a group of resistors joined in parallel equals the sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances, so the total resistance in a parallel circuit is decreased.

The two arrangements behave very differently. In a series circuit the current is constant throughout, so it is impracticable to connect an electric bulb and an electric heater in series, because they need currents of widely different values to operate properly. Another disadvantage of a series circuit is that when one component fails the circuit is broken and none of the components works, as you see when a single dead bulb in a string of fairy lights puts out the whole string. A parallel circuit, on the other hand, divides the current through the gadgets, which helps when each gadget has a different resistance and needs a different current.

sections.title: Heating effect of electric current
paragraphs: A cell or battery is a source of electrical energy, and to maintain a current the source keeps expending energy. Part of that energy may be used in useful work, like rotating the blades of an electric fan, and the rest may be expended as heat, which is why a fan becomes warm when used continuously for a long time.

If the electric circuit is purely resistive, that is, a configuration of resistors only connected to a battery, the source energy continually gets dissipated entirely in the form of heat. This is known as the heating effect of electric current, and it is used in devices such as electric heaters and electric irons.

Consider a current I flowing through a resistor of resistance R with a potential difference V across it, and let a charge Q flow in time t. The work done in moving the charge Q through the potential difference V is VQ, so the source must supply energy VQ in time t, and the power input to the circuit is P = VQ/t = VI. The energy supplied by the source in time t is therefore VIt, and this energy is dissipated in the resistor as heat, so H = VIt.

Applying Ohm's law V = IR to this gives H = I²Rt. This is Joule's law of heating, and it says that the heat produced in a resistor is directly proportional to the square of the current for a given resistance, directly proportional to the resistance for a given current, and directly proportional to the time for which the current flows.

paragraphs: The rate of doing work is power, and this is also the rate of consumption of energy. The rate at which electric energy is dissipated or consumed in an electric circuit is called electric power, and it is given by P = VI. Using Ohm's law this can also be written P = I²R or P = V²/R.

sections.title: Practice: mixed problems from the whole chapter
paragraphs: The questions below mix the ideas of the chapter. Work each one on paper first: write down what is given, choose the relation that connects the given quantities, and only then substitute numbers.

Before you plug in values, ask which quantity stays the same. In a series circuit it is the current; across a parallel combination it is the potential difference; for a fixed source voltage the heat and power go as 1/R.

spec.problem: A current of 0.5 A is drawn by a filament of an electric bulb for 10 minutes. Find the amount of electric charge that flows through the circuit.

steps.title: Write down what is given
steps.detail: Current I = 0.5 A. Time t = 10 minutes.

steps.title: Put the time in seconds
steps.detail: t = 10 min = 10 × 60 s = 600 s, because the ampere is coulombs per second.

steps.title: Use the definition of current
steps.detail: I = Q/t, so Q = I × t.

spec.answer: The amount of charge that flows through the circuit is 300 C.

spec.question: What does an electric circuit mean?
options: A continuous and closed path of an electric current
A path that is broken at the switch
Any piece of metal that carries charge
The flow of electrons from the positive terminal to the negative terminal
spec.answer: A continuous and closed path of an electric current
spec.explanation: A switch makes a conducting link between the cell and the bulb, so the path must be closed; if the circuit is broken anywhere the current stops and the bulb does not glow. Note also that electrons are negative, so the conventional current is taken opposite to the direction of electron flow, not along it.
spec.expected_understanding: The learner knows that a circuit must be a closed loop and does not confuse the direction of conventional current with the direction of electron flow.

spec.question: Calculate the number of electrons constituting one coulomb of charge.
spec.explanation: One electron carries a charge of 1.6 × 10^-19 C. So the number of electrons in 1 C is 1 / (1.6 × 10^-19), which is about 6.25 × 10^18, that is nearly 6 × 10^18 electrons. This is exactly why one coulomb is said to be the charge contained in nearly 6 × 10^18 electrons.
spec.expected_understanding: The learner can move between the charge on one electron and the charge of one coulomb.

paragraphs: Charges do not flow in a copper wire by themselves, just as water in a perfectly horizontal tube does not flow. If one end of the tube is joined to a tank kept at a higher level, so that there is a pressure difference between the two ends, water flows out of the other end.

For charges in a metallic wire, gravity has no role to play. The electrons move only if there is a difference of electric pressure, called the potential difference, along the conductor. A battery, made of one or more cells, produces this difference.

The chemical action within a cell generates the potential difference across its terminals even when no current is drawn from it. When the cell is connected to a conducting circuit element, the potential difference sets the charges in motion and produces an electric current, and to keep the current flowing the cell has to expend its stored chemical energy.

The potential difference between two points in a circuit carrying some current is the work done to move a unit charge from one point to the other, so V = W/Q. Its SI unit is the volt (V): one volt is the potential difference between two points when 1 joule of work is done to move a charge of 1 coulomb, that is 1 V = 1 J C^-1.
The voltmeter measures potential difference, and it is always connected in parallel across the points between which the potential difference is to be measured.

spec.problem: How much work is done in moving a charge of 2 C across two points having a potential difference 12 V?

steps.title: Write down what is given
steps.detail: Charge Q = 2 C, potential difference V = 12 V.

steps.title: Use the definition of potential difference
steps.detail: V = W/Q, so the work done is W = V × Q.

spec.answer: The work done is 24 J.

spec.question: How much energy is given to each coulomb of charge passing through a 6 V battery?
spec.answer: 6 J
spec.explanation: One volt means one joule of work per coulomb, so a 6 V battery gives 6 J of energy to every coulomb that passes through it. The battery is the device that maintains this potential difference across the conductor.
spec.expected_understanding: The learner reads the volt as joules per coulomb and can turn a potential difference into energy per unit charge.

paragraphs: A circuit contains a cell or a battery, a plug key, the electrical components and connecting wires. Instead of drawing the real objects, we draw a schematic diagram in which each component is replaced by a conventional symbol.

The symbols you will meet are: an electric cell; a battery, which is a combination of cells; a plug key or switch, shown open or closed; a wire joint; wires crossing without joining; an electric bulb; a resistor of resistance R; a variable resistance or rheostat; an ammeter; and a voltmeter.

Two of these symbols carry a rule with them. The ammeter goes in series with the part whose current you are measuring, and the voltmeter goes in parallel with the part whose potential difference you are measuring.

spec.question: How is a voltmeter connected in the circuit to measure the potential difference between two points?
options: In parallel across the two points
spec.answer: In parallel across the two points
spec.explanation: A voltmeter is always connected in parallel across the points between which the potential difference is to be measured. The ammeter is the one that goes in series, because it must carry the current it is measuring.
spec.expected_understanding: The learner keeps the two instruments and their connection rules apart.

paragraphs: Set up a circuit with a nichrome wire XY of length about 0.5 m, an ammeter, a voltmeter and four cells of 1.5 V each. Start with one cell and note the ammeter reading I and the voltmeter reading V across XY; then repeat with two, three and four cells. For each pair, work out V/I, and plot V against I.
In the activity you find approximately the same value of V/I in every case, and the V-I graph is a straight line passing through the origin. So V/I is a constant ratio for that wire.

In 1827 the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm found the relationship between the current in a metallic wire and the potential difference across its ends. The potential difference V across the ends of a given metallic wire is directly proportional to the current I through it, provided its temperature remains the same. This is Ohm's law: V is proportional to I, so V/I = constant = R, and V = IR.

R is a constant for the given metallic wire at a given temperature and is called its resistance, the property of a conductor to resist the flow of charges through it. Its SI unit is the ohm (Ω). If the potential difference across a conductor is 1 V and the current through it is 1 A, its resistance is 1 Ω, that is 1 ohm = 1 volt/1 ampere.

Because V = IR can be written I = V/R, the current through a resistor is inversely proportional to its resistance: if the resistance is doubled the current gets halved. In many practical cases we need to increase or decrease the current, and a component used to regulate current without changing the voltage source is called a variable resistance; a device called a rheostat is often used in a circuit to change the resistance.

spec.title: V-I graph of a nichrome wire
spec.description: A nichrome wire is connected to a number of 1.5 V cells, with an ammeter and a voltmeter. Add cells and change the wire resistance, and watch where each (current, potential difference) point falls on the graph.
spec.learning_goal: See that every measured point lies on a straight line through the origin, so V/I stays constant: this is Ohm's law.

controls.label: Cells in the circuit (1.5 V each)

spec.default_behaviour: With one cell the graph shows a single point at V = 1.5 V and the current I = V/R for the chosen R. The straight line through the origin is drawn for the chosen R, and the readout shows V, I and the ratio V/I, which does not change when more cells are added.

spec.problem: (a) How much current will an electric bulb draw from a 220 V source, if the resistance of the bulb filament is 1200 Ω? (b) How much current will an electric heater coil draw from a 220 V source, if the resistance of the heater coil is 100 Ω?

steps.title: Write down what is given for the bulb
Use Ohm's law in the form I = V/R
Write down what is given for the heater

spec.answer: The bulb draws about 0.18 A and the heater coil draws 2.2 A from the same 220 V source. Note the difference of current drawn by a bulb and a heater from the same source: the smaller the resistance, the larger the current.

spec.problem: The potential difference between the terminals of an electric heater is 60 V when it draws a current of 4 A from the source. What current will the heater draw if the potential difference is increased to 120 V?

steps.title: Find the resistance first
steps.detail: The resistance of the heater stays the same. From Ohm's law, R = V/I = 60 V / 4 A = 15 Ω.

steps.title: Now change the potential difference
steps.detail: With V = 120 V and R = 15 Ω, the current is I = V/R.

spec.answer: The current through the heater becomes 8 A when the potential difference is doubled.

spec.question: When a 12 V battery is connected across an unknown resistor, there is a current of 2.5 mA in the circuit. Find the value of the resistance of the resistor, in ohms.
spec.explanation: First change the current to amperes: 2.5 mA = 2.5 × 10^-3 A. Then R = V/I = 12 V / (2.5 × 10^-3 A) = 4800 Ω.
spec.expected_understanding: The learner converts milliampere to ampere before using Ohm's law, and rearranges V = IR into R = V/I.

paragraphs: Take a circuit with a cell, an ammeter, a nichrome wire of length l and a plug key, and note the current. Now replace the wire with another nichrome wire of the same thickness but twice the length, and note the current again: the ammeter reading decreases to one-half.

Repeat with a thicker nichrome wire of the same length, so that its cross-sectional area is larger: the ammeter reading increases. Now use a copper wire of the same length and the same area of cross-section as the first nichrome wire, and the reading changes again.

These observations show that the resistance of a conductor depends on its length, on its area of cross-section, and on the nature of its material. Precise measurements show that the resistance of a uniform metallic conductor is directly proportional to its length l and inversely proportional to its area of cross-section A, so R = ρl/A.

The constant ρ (rho) is called the electrical resistivity of the material of the conductor. Its SI unit is Ω m, and it is a characteristic property of the material. Metals and alloys have very low resistivity, in the range 10^-8 Ω m to 10^-6 Ω m, and are good conductors of electricity; insulators like rubber and glass have resistivity of the order of 10^12 to 10^17 Ω m. Both the resistance and the resistivity of a material vary with temperature.

The resistivity of an alloy is generally higher than that of its constituent metals, and alloys do not oxidise (burn) readily at high temperatures; for this reason they are commonly used in electrical heating devices like electric irons and toasters. Tungsten is used almost exclusively for filaments of electric bulbs, while copper and aluminium are generally used for electrical transmission lines.

spec.problem: Resistance of a metal wire of length 1 m is 26 Ω at 20 degrees C. If the diameter of the wire is 0.3 mm, what will be the resistivity of the metal at that temperature? Using the table of resistivities, predict the material of the wire.

steps.title: Write down what is given
steps.detail: R = 26 Ω, length l = 1 m, diameter d = 0.3 mm = 3 × 10^-4 m.

steps.title: Find the area of cross-section
steps.detail: The wire is round, so A = πd²/4.

steps.title: Rearrange R = ρl/A
steps.detail: The resistivity is ρ = RA/l = Rπd²/(4l).

steps.title: Substitute
steps.detail: Putting in the values gives ρ = 1.84 × 10^-6 Ω m.

steps.title: Name the material
steps.detail: Looking at the table of resistivities at 20 degrees C, the value 1.84 × 10^-6 Ω m is the resistivity of manganese.

spec.answer: The resistivity of the metal at 20 degrees C is 1.84 × 10^-6 Ω m, which is the resistivity of manganese.

spec.problem: A wire of given material having length l and area of cross-section A has a resistance of 4 Ω. What would be the resistance of another wire of the same material having length l/2 and area of cross-section 2A?

steps.title: Write the first wire
steps.detail: For the first wire, R1 = ρl/A = 4 Ω.

steps.title: Write the second wire
steps.detail: For the second wire, R2 = ρ(l/2)/(2A) = (1/4) ρl/A.

spec.answer: The resistance of the new wire is 1 Ω.

spec.question: Will current flow more easily through a thick wire or a thin wire of the same material, when connected to the same source? Why?
options: A thick wire, because a larger area of cross-section gives a smaller resistance
A thin wire, because a smaller area of cross-section gives a smaller resistance
Both equally, because the material is the same
A thick wire, because the material of a thick wire has lower resistivity
spec.answer: A thick wire, because a larger area of cross-section gives a smaller resistance
spec.explanation: Resistance is inversely proportional to the area of cross-section, R = ρl/A. A thicker wire of the same material and length has the larger area, so its resistance is smaller and the current is larger. Resistivity depends on the material only, not on the thickness.
spec.expected_understanding: The learner separates resistance (which depends on size) from resistivity (which depends on material).

paragraphs: When three resistors R1, R2 and R3 are joined end to end, they are said to be connected in series. If you move the ammeter to any position in such a circuit, its reading does not change: in a series combination the current is the same in every part of the circuit, so the same current passes through each resistor.

Measure the potential difference across the whole combination and call it V, then measure the potential differences V1, V2 and V3 across the three resistors separately. You find that V = V1 + V2 + V3: the total potential difference across a series combination is the sum of the potential differences across the individual resistors.

Now replace the three resistors by one equivalent resistor of resistance R that carries the same current I with the same potential difference V across it, so that V = IR. Applying Ohm's law to the three resistors separately gives V1 = IR1, V2 = IR2 and V3 = IR3.

Putting these into V = V1 + V2 + V3 gives IR = IR1 + IR2 + IR3, and dividing by I gives Rs = R1 + R2 + R3. So when several resistors are joined in series, the resistance of the combination equals the sum of their individual resistances, and it is greater than any individual resistance.

steps.title: Start from the observed sum
steps.detail: The experiment shows the total potential difference is V = V1 + V2 + V3 across the series combination.

steps.title: Replace the combination by one resistor
steps.detail: Let one equivalent resistor R carry the same current I with the same total potential difference V, so Ohm's law for the whole circuit gives V = IR.

steps.title: Apply Ohm's law to each resistor
steps.detail: The current through each resistor is the same I, so V1 = IR1, V2 = IR2 and V3 = IR3.

steps.title: Substitute and cancel I
steps.detail: IR = IR1 + IR2 + IR3, and dividing both sides by I gives Rs = R1 + R2 + R3.

steps.title: Read the result
steps.detail: The equivalent resistance is the plain sum, so it is larger than any single resistance in the combination.

spec.problem: An electric lamp, whose resistance is 20 Ω, and a conductor of 4 Ω resistance are connected to a 6 V battery. Calculate (a) the total resistance of the circuit, (b) the current through the circuit, and (c) the potential difference across the electric lamp and conductor.

steps.title: Add the series resistances
steps.detail: The lamp R1 = 20 Ω and the conductor R2 = 4 Ω are in series, so Rs = 20 Ω + 4 Ω = 24 Ω.

steps.title: Find the current
steps.detail: The battery gives V = 6 V, so I = V/Rs = 6 V / 24 Ω = 0.25 A. This same current flows through both.

steps.title: Potential difference across the conductor
steps.detail: V2 = R2 × I = 4 Ω × 0.25 A = 1 V. Check: 5 V + 1 V = 6 V, the battery voltage.

steps.title: Check the equivalent resistance
steps.detail: A single resistor replacing the two must give 0.25 A at 6 V, so R = V/I = 6 V / 0.25 A = 24 Ω, the same as the total series resistance.

spec.answer: Total resistance 24 Ω, current 0.25 A, potential difference 5 V across the lamp and 1 V across the conductor.

spec.question: A battery of three cells of 2 V each is connected in series with a 5 Ω resistor, an 8 Ω resistor, a 12 Ω resistor and a plug key. What current flows through the resistors? Give the answer in amperes.
spec.explanation: Three cells of 2 V each give 6 V. The series resistance is 5 + 8 + 12 = 25 Ω. So I = V/Rs = 6 V / 25 Ω = 0.24 A, and this same current flows through every resistor. A voltmeter connected across the 12 Ω resistor would read 12 Ω × 0.24 A = 2.88 V.
spec.expected_understanding: The learner adds the cell voltages, adds the resistances in series, and applies Ohm's law once for the whole circuit.

paragraphs: When three resistors are connected together between the same two points X and Y, they are said to be connected in parallel. Now the potential difference across each resistor is the same, but the current divides.

Measure the total current I entering the combination, and then the separate currents I1, I2 and I3 through the three branches. You find I = I1 + I2 + I3: the total current is the sum of the separate currents through each branch of the combination.
Let Rp be the equivalent resistance of the parallel combination. Applying Ohm's law to the whole combination gives I = V/Rp, and applying it to each resistor gives I1 = V/R1, I2 = V/R2 and I3 = V/R3.

Substituting these into I = I1 + I2 + I3 gives V/Rp = V/R1 + V/R2 + V/R3, and dividing by V gives 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. The reciprocal of the equivalent resistance of a group of resistors joined in parallel equals the sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances, so the total resistance in a parallel circuit is decreased.

The two arrangements behave very differently. In a series circuit the current is constant throughout, so it is impracticable to connect an electric bulb and an electric heater in series, because they need currents of widely different values to operate properly. Another disadvantage of a series circuit is that when one component fails the circuit is broken and none of the components works, as you see when a single dead bulb in a string of fairy lights puts out the whole string. A parallel circuit, on the other hand, divides the current through the gadgets, which helps when each gadget has a different resistance and needs a different current.

steps.title: Start from the observed sum
steps.detail: The experiment shows the total current is I = I1 + I2 + I3 into the parallel combination.

steps.title: Replace the combination by one resistor
steps.detail: Let one equivalent resistor Rp carry the same total current I at the same potential difference V, so I = V/Rp.

steps.title: Apply Ohm's law to each branch
steps.detail: Every branch has the same potential difference V, so I1 = V/R1, I2 = V/R2 and I3 = V/R3.

spec.problem: Three resistors R1, R2 and R3 have the values 5 Ω, 10 Ω and 30 Ω respectively, and are connected in parallel to a battery of 12 V. Calculate (a) the current through each resistor, (b) the total current in the circuit, and (c) the total circuit resistance.

steps.title: Note the potential difference
steps.detail: The battery gives V = 12 V, and this is also the potential difference across each individual resistor because they are in parallel.

spec.answer: The branch currents are 2.4 A, 1.2 A and 0.4 A; the total current is 4 A; the total resistance of the parallel combination is 3 Ω.

spec.problem: In a circuit with a 12 V battery, R1 = 10 Ω and R2 = 40 Ω are in parallel with each other, and R3 = 30 Ω, R4 = 20 Ω and R5 = 60 Ω are in parallel with each other; the two parallel groups are joined in series. Calculate (a) the total resistance in the circuit and (b) the total current flowing in the circuit.

steps.title: Add the two groups in series
steps.detail: The total resistance is R = R' + R'' = 8 Ω + 10 Ω = 18 Ω.

steps.title: Find the total current
steps.detail: By Ohm's law, I = V/R = 12 V / 18 Ω = 0.67 A.

spec.answer: The total resistance is 18 Ω and the total current is about 0.67 A.

spec.question: What are the advantages of connecting electrical devices in parallel with the battery instead of connecting them in series?
options: Each device works with the full source voltage and independently, and the total resistance of the circuit decreases
The same current flows through every device
When one device fails, all the other devices stop working
The total resistance of the circuit increases as more devices are added
spec.answer: Each device works with the full source voltage and independently, and the total resistance of the circuit decreases
spec.explanation: In a parallel circuit every gadget gets the same potential difference and its own current, which suits gadgets of different resistances, and the total resistance is decreased. In a series circuit a single failure breaks the circuit and nothing works, which is why series wiring is not used for domestic circuits.
spec.expected_understanding: The learner can compare series and parallel circuits by current, voltage and behaviour on failure.

paragraphs: A cell or battery is a source of electrical energy, and to maintain a current the source keeps expending energy. Part of that energy may be used in useful work, like rotating the blades of an electric fan, and the rest may be expended as heat, which is why a fan becomes warm when used continuously for a long time.

If the electric circuit is purely resistive, that is, a configuration of resistors only connected to a battery, the source energy continually gets dissipated entirely in the form of heat. This is known as the heating effect of electric current, and it is used in devices such as electric heaters and electric irons.

Consider a current I flowing through a resistor of resistance R with a potential difference V across it, and let a charge Q flow in time t. The work done in moving the charge Q through the potential difference V is VQ, so the source must supply energy VQ in time t, and the power input to the circuit is P = VQ/t = VI. The energy supplied by the source in time t is therefore VIt, and this energy is dissipated in the resistor as heat, so H = VIt.

Applying Ohm's law V = IR to this gives H = I²Rt. This is Joule's law of heating, and it says that the heat produced in a resistor is directly proportional to the square of the current for a given resistance, directly proportional to the resistance for a given current, and directly proportional to the time for which the current flows.

spec.title: From H = VIt to Joule's law H = I²Rt

steps.title: Energy supplied by the source
steps.detail: In time t a charge Q flows, and the work done in moving it through the potential difference V is VQ, so the source supplies energy VQ in time t.

steps.title: Write the power input
steps.detail: Since I = Q/t, the power input is P = VQ/t = VI, so the energy supplied in time t is VIt.

steps.title: This energy becomes heat
steps.detail: In a purely resistive circuit the whole of it is dissipated in the resistor as heat, so H = VIt.

steps.title: Use Ohm's law to remove V
steps.detail: Put V = IR into H = VIt, giving H = (IR)It = I²Rt.

steps.title: Read the three proportionalities
steps.detail: For a fixed resistance, heat goes as the square of the current; for a fixed current, heat goes as the resistance; and for both fixed, heat goes as the time.

spec.problem: An electric iron consumes energy at a rate of 840 W when heating is at the maximum rate and 360 W when the heating is at the minimum. The voltage is 220 V. What are the current and the resistance in each case?

steps.title: Start from the power relation
steps.detail: The power input is P = VI, so the current is I = P/V, and the resistance follows from R = V/I.

spec.answer: At the maximum rate the current is 3.82 A and the resistance is 57.60 Ω; at the minimum rate the current is 1.64 A and the resistance is 134.15 Ω.

spec.problem: 100 J of heat is produced each second in a 4 Ω resistance. Find the potential difference across the resistor.

steps.title: Write down what is given
steps.detail: Heat H = 100 J, resistance R = 4 Ω, time t = 1 s. We want V.

steps.title: Use Joule's law to get the current
steps.detail: H = I²Rt, so I = square root of (H / (Rt)) = square root of (100 J / (4 Ω × 1 s)) = 5 A.

steps.title: Find the potential difference
steps.detail: From Ohm's law V = IR = 5 A × 4 Ω = 20 V.

spec.answer: The potential difference across the resistor is 20 V.

spec.question: An electric iron of resistance 20 Ω takes a current of 5 A. Calculate the heat developed in 30 s. Give the answer in joules.
spec.explanation: Use Joule's law H = I²Rt = (5 A)² × 20 Ω × 30 s = 25 × 20 × 30 = 15000 J.
spec.expected_understanding: The learner squares the current and multiplies by resistance and time.

paragraphs: The generation of heat in a conductor is an inevitable consequence of electric current, and in many cases it is undesirable because useful electrical energy turns into heat and the components heat up. But the heating effect has many useful applications: the electric laundry iron, electric toaster, electric oven, electric kettle and electric heater are all based on Joule's heating.

The electric bulb uses heating to produce light. The filament must retain as much of the generated heat as possible so that it becomes very hot and emits light, and it must not melt at that temperature. A strong metal with a high melting point, such as tungsten (melting point 3380 °C), is used for bulb filaments, the filament is thermally isolated as much as possible using insulating supports, and the bulb is filled with chemically inactive nitrogen and argon gases to prolong the life of the filament. Most of the power consumed by the filament appears as heat, and only a small part is radiated as light.

The fuse is another common application of Joule's heating. It protects circuits and appliances by stopping the flow of any unduly high current, and it is placed in series with the device. It consists of a piece of wire made of a metal or an alloy of appropriate melting point, for example aluminium, copper, iron or lead, usually encased in a cartridge of porcelain or similar material with metal ends. If a current larger than the specified value flows, the temperature of the fuse wire rises, the wire melts and the circuit is broken.

Fuses for domestic purposes are rated 1 A, 2 A, 3 A, 5 A, 10 A, and so on, and the rating has to be chosen from the current the appliance draws. For an electric iron which consumes 1 kW electric power when operated at 220 V, a current of (1000/220) A, that is 4.54 A, will flow in the circuit. In this case a 5 A fuse must be used: the fuse wire melts only when a current larger than its specified value flows, so the rating must lie above the working current of 4.54 A, and 3 A would be too low.

spec.question: An electric iron consumes 1 kW of electric power when operated at 220 V. Which fuse rating must be used with it?
spec.answer: 5 A
spec.explanation: A current of (1000/220) A, that is 4.54 A, flows in the circuit. The fuse wire melts only when a current larger than its specified value flows, so a 3 A fuse would be below the working current and a 5 A fuse must be used.
spec.expected_understanding: The learner works out the working current of the appliance and picks the fuse rating that lies just above it instead of below it.

paragraphs: The rate of doing work is power, and this is also the rate of consumption of energy. The rate at which electric energy is dissipated or consumed in an electric circuit is called electric power, and it is given by P = VI. Using Ohm's law this can also be written P = I²R or P = V²/R.
The SI unit of electric power is the watt (W). It is the power consumed by a device that carries 1 A of current when operated at a potential difference of 1 V, so 1 W = 1 volt × 1 ampere = 1 V A.

The watt is a very small unit, so in actual practice we use a much larger unit called the kilowatt, which is equal to 1000 watts. Electrical energy is the product of power and time, so its unit is the watt hour (W h), the energy consumed when 1 watt of power is used for 1 hour. The commercial unit of electric energy is the kilowatt hour (kW h), commonly known as a unit: 1 kW h = 1000 watt × 3600 second = 3.6 × 10^6 watt second = 3.6 × 10^6 joule.

One caution: many people think that electrons are consumed in an electric circuit. This is wrong. We pay the electricity board or electric company to provide energy to move electrons through gadgets like the electric bulb, fan and engines; we pay for the energy that we use.

spec.problem: An electric bulb is connected to a 220 V generator. The current is 0.50 A. What is the power of the bulb?

steps.title: Use the power relation
steps.detail: P = VI.

spec.answer: The power of the bulb is 110 W.

spec.problem: An electric refrigerator rated 400 W operates 8 hour/day. What is the cost of the energy to operate it for 30 days at Rs 3.00 per kW h?

steps.title: Find the total energy in watt hours
steps.detail: 400 W × 8.0 hour/day × 30 days = 96000 W h.

steps.title: Convert to kilowatt hours
steps.detail: 96000 W h = 96 kW h, since 1 kW h = 1000 W h.

steps.title: Multiply by the rate
steps.detail: 96 kW h × Rs 3.00 per kW h = Rs 288.00.

spec.answer: The cost of running the refrigerator for 30 days is Rs 288.00.

spec.question: Which of the following terms does not represent electrical power in a circuit?
spec.answer: IR²
spec.explanation: Electric power is P = VI, which becomes P = I²R when V = IR is put in, and P = V²/R when I = V/R is put in. The combination IR² has the wrong powers of I and R, so it is not a power.
spec.expected_understanding: The learner can move between the three forms of the power relation and recognise a wrong one.

spec.question: A piece of wire of resistance R is cut into five equal parts. These parts are then connected in parallel. If the equivalent resistance of this combination is R', then what is the ratio R/R'?
spec.explanation: Each of the five equal parts has resistance R/5. Five such resistors in parallel have 1/R' = 5/(R/5) = 25/R, so R' = R/25. Therefore R/R' = 25.
spec.expected_understanding: The learner combines the effect of cutting a wire (length falls, so resistance falls) with the parallel rule.

spec.question: An electric bulb is rated 220 V and 100 W. When it is operated on 110 V, what power will it consume?
spec.explanation: The resistance of the bulb is fixed: R = V²/P = (220 V)² / 100 W = 484 Ω. At 110 V the power is P = V²/R = (110 V)² / 484 Ω = 25 W. Halving the voltage quarters the power, because power goes as V² for a fixed resistance.
spec.expected_understanding: The learner finds the resistance from the rating and then recomputes the power at the new voltage.

spec.question: Two conducting wires of the same material and of equal lengths and equal diameters are first connected in series and then in parallel in a circuit across the same potential difference. What is the ratio of the heat produced in the series combination to that in the parallel combination?
spec.explanation: Each wire has resistance R. In series the resistance is 2R; in parallel it is R/2. For the same potential difference V and the same time t, the heat is V²t/R, so it is inversely proportional to the resistance. The ratio of heats is (1/2R) : (1/(R/2)) = 1 : 4.
spec.expected_understanding: The learner sees that for a fixed source voltage, a smaller resistance produces more heat.

spec.question: How many 176 Ω resistors (in parallel) are required to carry 5 A on a 220 V line?
spec.explanation: The combination must have resistance R = V/I = 220 V / 5 A = 44 Ω. If n resistors of 176 Ω are joined in parallel, R = 176/n, so n = 176/44 = 4.
spec.expected_understanding: The learner works backwards from the required current to the required equivalent resistance, then uses the parallel rule for identical resistors.
